‼️if you are visiting Venice this year👇🏻 

🤍 Follow for more unique places and travel guides around the world

Getting there

Fly into Venice Marco Polo Airport. From there, you can take a water taxi (expensive but iconic) or the Alilaguna water bus (budget-friendly). 

If you’re coming by train, Venezia Santa Lucia drops you straight into the heart of the city.

Where to stay

If it’s your first time, stay near San Marco or along the Grand Canal so you can walk everywhere early in the morning before crowds take over.

🤍 I stayed at the @stregisvenice and it was an epic experience. One of my favorite moments of staying here was that every evening they carry on a ritual called champagne sabering - where a bottle is opened with a sword (yes, an actual sword) and I actually got to do it myself and then try it 🤍

Things to do

Get lost. Not even kidding! Venice is best experienced with no plan
Wake up early and walk through Piazza San Marco before 8 AM
Take a vaporetto or gondola ride down the Grand Canal
Visit Burano for colorful houses or Murano for glassmaking
Climb the Campanile for one of the best views in the city

What to eat

Skip the tourist places right by the main squares.
Walk a few streets away and look for smaller, local spots.
Try cicchetti (Venetian tapas), fresh pasta, and tiramisu (this is where it was born).
Also, don’t leave without having a spritz by the water.

Things no one tells you ⚠️

Venice is beautiful, but it’s also crowded. Early mornings and late evenings are your best friend
Restaurants near major attractions are often overpriced and not worth it
Pack light! There are a LOT of bridges and no Ubers here
Acqua alta (flooding) can happen, especially in certain months, so check ahead

‼️You don’t always need a car to explore European towns. There are plenty of car-free villages that can only be explored on foot for the most part

🤍 follow for more unique places around the world @tripuntraveled 

Here are 5 car free places in Europe worth adding to your list

🏔️ Zermatt, Switzerland
A mountain village beneath the Matterhorn where regular cars are not allowed. Explore the center on foot, then take the mountain trains and cable cars for some of the most dramatic views in Switzerland.

🚤 Giethoorn, Netherlands
Known for its canals, tiny bridges, and thatched cottages. The old village is best explored by walking along the narrow paths or taking a small boat through the canals.

🏰 Pérouges, France
A medieval hilltop village filled with uneven cobblestones, stone houses, and streets that feel almost untouched by time. Come early.

🌿 Pienza, Italy
A small Renaissance town overlooking the rolling hills of Val d’Orcia. Walk the panoramic streets, stop for pecorino cheese, and stay for sunset over the Tuscan countryside.

🌸 Óbidos, Portugal
A whitewashed medieval town wrapped inside castle walls. Walk through the flower covered streets, walk along the walls, and try the local cherry liqueur served in a chocolate cup.

I road tripped across the entire Lofoten Islands in winter, and there are a few things I wish someone had told me before I arrived.

❄️ Winter weather changes by the hour. A road that’s perfectly clear can turn into a snowstorm 20 minutes later.

🚗 Renting a car is the best way to explore. Public transport exists, but you’ll miss a lot of the islands’ most incredible viewpoints.

💳 You barely need cash. Almost everywhere accepts cards.

🌅 Don’t expect long daylight hours. In winter, you only get a few hours of usable light, so plan your route carefully.

🏡 Stay in a traditional rorbu if you can. Sleeping in an old fishermen’s cabin is one of the most memorable parts of the experience.

🥾 Many famous hikes aren’t possible in winter unless you’re experienced and properly equipped. The scenery is still unbelievable without them.

No photo or video prepared me for how quiet these islands feel. Once you leave the main towns, it’s just mountains, fishing villages, and a silence that’s almost impossible to describe.

📍 Lofoten Islands, Norway 🇳🇴

This tiny Tuscan hilltop town was redesigned by a Pope who was obsessed with creating a perfect city during the Renaissance in the 1400s.

The entire town was carefully planned with symmetry and perspective. The alleyways open into perfectly framed Tuscan countryside views over the Val d’Orcia making it one of the earliest examples of urban planning in Europe. 

Streets here are named after love, kisses, luck, and dreams as a reminder of humanity and hope…and they’re tucked so quietly into the town that you’ll miss them if you’re not paying attention.

This is…

📍 Pienza, Tuscany, Italy

🚗 How to get here
It is easily accessible by car as part of a Val d’Orcia road trip or you can also take a train to Montepulciano and drive from there.

🧀 What to eat
Pienza is famous for pecorino cheese. You’ll find shops all over the town with tastings, including aged and truffle variations.

This city was once one of the richest places on Earth and thrived as one of Europe’s most important trading hubs. 

Ships from across the continent sailed into its canals, bringing wealth that transformed it into a medieval powerhouse.

Then the waterways slowly silted up, trade moved elsewhere, money disappeared, and then centuries of decline while the rest of Europe modernized around it.

Now there are medieval towers, cobblestone streets, hidden canals, horse drawn carriages, and some of the most beautiful architecture in Europe almost exactly as it looked hundreds of years ago.

This is…

📍 Bruges, Belgium

🚗 How to get here
Bruges is about 1 hour by train from Brussels and an easy day trip, though I’d recommend staying overnight to experience the city after the crowds leave.

🍫 What to eat
Belgian waffles, fresh fries, local chocolates, and a warm bowl of Flemish beef stew.

Most people have heard of Paris but may not have heard of Paris Syndrome and I learned about it recently…but it’s a real phenomenon.

The term became famous after some Japanese tourists experienced severe culture shock when visiting Paris.

Many were expecting the city they had seen in movies, advertisements, and magazines with elegant streets, fashionable locals, romance around every corner, and a picture perfect atmosphere.

Instead, they found -
traffic
crowds
graffiti
pickpockets
cigarette smell
and people trying to get to work

For some visitors, the gap between expectation and reality became so overwhelming that they experienced symptoms like anxiety, panic, dizziness, and extreme distress.

Psychologists eventually gave the phenomenon a name and called it Paris Syndrome.

The funny thing is that Paris isn’t the problem. The problem is expecting a real city to live up to a fantasy.
